label: Blue Note
rationale: The first record by the quintet everyone means when they say 'the Horace Silver Quintet' — Blue Mitchell, Junior Cook, Gene Taylor, Louis Hayes — and the date on which Silver's own composing book and that band's chemistry arrive together [S1, S2] (obs). AllMusic's Steve Huey calls it 'one of Silver's all-time classics' and 'everything small-group hard bop should be, and a terrific example of what made the Blue Note label's mainstream sound so infectious' [S1] (obs); the review table gives it 5/5 at AllMusic and 5/5 in the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide [S2] (obs). Defining statement: eight Silver originals, no standards — 'Juicy Lucy', 'Come on Home', 'Swingin' the Samba' and 'Cookin' at the Continental' all enter the book here, and 'Cookin' at the Continental' becomes a hard-bop standard that later bands keep playing [S1, S2] (obs). Lineage: it sits one session before Blowin' the Blues Away in the same year and establishes the quintet that carries Silver's Blue Note sound through 1964 [S2] (inf). Session gravity: three of these five — Mitchell, Cook, Hayes — are the working band, not pickup players; Silver's group was the proving ground for hard-bop rhythm-section practice [S1, S3] (inf). It still plays: the record's pleasure is exactly its gregariousness — concise solos, tight heads, blues grounding — which is the discovery test passed rather than argued [S1] (inf). Not oversold: this is a strong second-tier classic rather than a consensus-core monument; the case rests on AllMusic and the Rolling Stone guide plus the band's place in Silver's arc, not on a deep stack of independent canon lists [S2] (obs). One documented naming note: AllMusic and Wikipedia print the title as 'Finger Poppin' with the Horace Silver Quintet'; the album is catalogued here under the short title, which is the form both the Blue Note cover and jazzdisco use [S1, S3] (obs).

personnel_record.notes: One session, one room: Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack, NJ, 31 January 1959 (jazzdisco matrices tk.11-tk.39; Wikipedia agrees). CONFLICT RECORDED, not smoothed: AllMusic dates the session 1 February 1959 and gives the location as 'New York, NY / Van Gelder Studios, Hackensack, NJ' on two lines — the Hackensack room is what all three sources name, and the date used here is jazzdisco's 31 January, the session-level authority; AllMusic's one-day-later date is left standing in this note because it cannot be adjudicated from the sources gathered. Either date falls before Van Gelder's July 1959 move, so the place slug is unaffected. Track order follows Wikipedia and AllMusic (the released LP sequence); jazzdisco numbers the same eight matrices in a different order (Cookin' at the Continental tk.11 first, Juicy Lucy tk.39 last), which is matrix order rather than album order. AllMusic's page also lists a 1 February 1959 release date, while Wikipedia cites Billboard's 27 April 1959 review of new releases and an April 1959 issue; the album is catalogued at year 1959 either way. No alternate takes or bonus tracks are included: the 2003 Rudy Van Gelder Edition on Apple carries the same eight titles.

ballot.case_for: The debut recording of Silver's celebrated Mitchell–Cook–Taylor–Hayes quintet presents eight Silver originals, making it a defining document of his blues-grounded compositional language and disciplined working-band interplay rather than another interchangeable blowing session (S1–S3). AllMusic calls it one of Silver's all-time classics and an exemplary small-group hard-bop record; the dossier also reports five-star assessments from AllMusic and The Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide (S1, S2). Its infectious ensemble writing, contrasting trio feature on 'Sweet Stuff,' and enduring 'Cookin' at the Continental' give it both immediate discovery value and a concrete repertoire legacy (S1–S3).
ballot.case_against: The evidence establishes enthusiastic critical approval more securely than broad canonical consensus: Wikipedia repeats AllMusic's rating, while sessionographies and identifier sources do not supply additional independent critical judgments. The band's debut is historically meaningful, but that does not by itself establish this album as a definitive statement alongside Blowin' the Blues Away; its distinct contribution must rest on the music and repertoire, not simply chronological priority. Claims that this particular session established hard-bop rhythm-section practice or anchored an unchanged lineup through 1964 exceed what the dossier demonstrates.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give this strong, contested candidate a focused listen for its distinctive compositional and ensemble achievement, rather than treating either its debut status or its proximity to better-known Silver landmarks as decisive.
